claim: Cholecystokinin (cck)-expressing cells in the hypothalamic dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMd) are necessary for initiating escape from innate threats via a projection to the dorsolateral periaqueductal gray (dlPAG).
source: Cholecystokinin (cck)-expressing cells in the hypothalamic dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMd) are necessary for initiating escape from innate threats via a projection to the dorsolateral periaqueductal gray (dlPAG).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (implied by the context of the abstract introducing previous findings).

claim: PMd-cck cells are activated during escape, but not other defensive behaviors.
source: We now show that in mice PMd-cck cells are activated during escape, but not other defensive behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2).

claim: PMd-cck ensemble activity can predict future escape.
source: PMd-cck ensemble activity can also predict future escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 3H).

claim: PMd inhibition decreases escape speed from both innate and conditioned threats.
source: Furthermore, PMd inhibition decreases escape speed from both innate and conditioned threats.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 5).

claim: Inhibition of the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG decreased escape speed.
source: Inhibition of the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG also decreased escape speed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 8).

claim: PMd-cck and dlPAG activity in mice showed higher mutual information during exposure to innate and conditioned threats.
source: Intriguingly, PMd-cck and dlPAG activity in mice showed higher mutual information during exposure to innate and conditioned threats.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 9).

claim: A posterior hypothalamic-to-dlPAG pathway in humans increased activity during exposure to aversive images.
source: In parallel, human functional magnetic resonance imaging data show that a posterior hypothalamic-to-dlPAG pathway increased activity during exposure to aversive images, indicating that a similar pathway may possibly have a related role in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human fMRI studies presented in the manuscript (Figure 10).

claim: The PMd-dlPAG circuit is a central node controlling escape vigor elicited by both innate and conditioned threats.
source: Our data identify the PMd-dlPAG circuit as a central node, controlling escape vigor elicited by both innate and conditioned threats.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data from multiple experiments in the manuscript.

claim: The dlPAG controls escape vigor, measured by escape velocity.
source: In agreement with these data, it has been shown that the dlPAG controls escape vigor, measured by escape velocity (Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Evans et al., 2018.

claim: Stimulation of the dlPAG provokes rapid escape in rodents.
source: Stimulation of the dlPAG provokes rapid escape in rodents (Deng et al., 2016; Evans et al., 2018) and panic-related symptoms in humans (Nashold et al., 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Deng et al., 2016 and Evans et al., 2018.

claim: Stimulation of the dlPAG provokes panic-related symptoms in humans.
source: Stimulation of the dlPAG provokes rapid escape in rodents (Deng et al., 2016; Evans et al., 2018) and panic-related symptoms in humans (Nashold et al., 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Nashold et al., 1969.

claim: A high proportion of dlPAG cells are activated during escape.
source: Furthermore, single-unit dlPAG recordings show that a high proportion of cells are activated during escape (Deng et al., 2016; Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Deng et al., 2016 and Evans et al., 2018.

claim: The dorsomedial portion of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMHdm) is a major excitatory dlPAG input.
source: The dorsomedial portion of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMHdm) is a major excitatory dlPAG input, suggesting that the VMHdm projection may mediate escape.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Activation of the VMHdm projection to the dlPAG caused freezing, not escape.
source: However, activation of the VMHdm projection to the dlPAG surprisingly caused freezing, not escape (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Wang et al., 2015.

claim: The dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMd) is the other main hypothalamic input to the dlPAG.
source: The other main hypothalamic input to the dlPAG is the dorsal premammillary nucleus (PMd) (Canteras and Swanson, 1992; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Canteras and Swanson, 1992 and Tovote et al., 2016.

claim: The PMd is the strongest known input to the panicogenic dlPAG.
source: Surprisingly, despite being the strongest known input to the panicogenic dlPAG (Canteras and Swanson, 1992; Tovote et al., 2016), the activity of this nucleus has not been directly manipulated or recorded.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Canteras and Swanson, 1992 and Tovote et al., 2016.

claim: The PMd is a key component of the hypothalamic defense system and is strongly activated by various imminent threats.
source: The PMd is a key component of the hypothalamic defense system and is strongly activated by various imminent threats (Cezario et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Cezario et al., 2008.

claim: Carbon dioxide activates the rodent PMd.
source: Dangerous stimuli that activate the rodent PMd are extremely diverse and include carbon dioxide (Johnson et al., 2011), several predators (cats, snakes, and ferrets) (Mendes-Gomes et al., 2020), as well as aversive lights and noises (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Johnson et al., 2011.

claim: Several predators (cats, snakes, and ferrets) activate the rodent PMd.
source: Dangerous stimuli that activate the rodent PMd are extremely diverse and include carbon dioxide (Johnson et al., 2011), several predators (cats, snakes, and ferrets) (Mendes-Gomes et al., 2020), as well as aversive lights and noises (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Mendes-Gomes et al., 2020.

claim: Aversive lights and noises activate the rodent PMd.
source: Dangerous stimuli that activate the rodent PMd are extremely diverse and include carbon dioxide (Johnson et al., 2011), several predators (cats, snakes, and ferrets) (Mendes-Gomes et al., 2020), as well as aversive lights and noises (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Kim et al., 2017.

claim: The PMd is activated by contexts fear-conditioned with shocks.
source: Additionally, the PMd is also activated by contexts fear-conditioned with shocks (Canteras et al., 2008) and social defeat (Faturi et al., 2014), indicating that it may play a role in coordinating defensive behaviors to both innate and conditioned threats.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Canteras et al., 2008.

claim: The PMd is activated by social defeat.
source: Additionally, the PMd is also activated by contexts fear-conditioned with shocks (Canteras et al., 2008) and social defeat (Faturi et al., 2014), indicating that it may play a role in coordinating defensive behaviors to both innate and conditioned threats.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Faturi et al., 2014.

claim: The vast majority of PMd cells are glutamatergic and express cholecystokinin (cck).
source: The vast majority of PMd cells are glutamatergic and express cholecystokinin (cck), and we recently showed that these cells controlled versatile context-specific escape from innate threats (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Wang et al., 2021.

claim: PMd-cck cells controlled versatile context-specific escape from innate threats.
source: The vast majority of PMd cells are glutamatergic and express cholecystokinin (cck), and we recently showed that these cells controlled versatile context-specific escape from innate threats (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Inhibition of the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG decreased the number of observed escapes induced by a range of innate threats, including a live predator and carbon dioxide.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG decreased the number of observed escapes induced by a range of innate threats, including a live predator and carbon dioxide.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Wang et al., 2021 (implied by context).

claim: The PMd-cck projection to the anteromedial thalamus (amv) was only recruited for escapes that required spatial navigation.
source: Conversely, the PMd-cck projection to the anteromedial thalamus (amv) was only recruited for escapes that required spatial navigation (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Wang et al., 2021.

claim: PMd-cck cells were active during escapes.
source: We previously also showed that PMd-cck cells were active during escapes (Wang et al., 2021), but it remains unknown if these cells encode or predict future occurrences of escape and other defensive behaviors, and whether they represent relevant metrics such as distance to threat.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Innate and conditioned threats induce distance from the threat source, freezing, and stretch-attend postures.
source: Threat exposure induced distance from the threat source, freezing, and stretch-attend postures (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mean freeze bout duration was 2.03 s ± 0.15.
source: (The mean freeze bout duration was 2.03 s ± 0.15.)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: During exposure to threat, approach velocity was lower relative to control assays.
source: Additionally, relative to control assays, during exposure to threat, approach velocity was lower, while escape velocity was higher (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: During exposure to threat, escape velocity was higher relative to control assays.
source: Additionally, relative to control assays, during exposure to threat, approach velocity was lower, while escape velocity was higher (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Mice slowly and cautiously approach threats and then escape in high velocity back to safer locations far from threats.
source: These results indicate that mice slowly and cautiously approach threats and then escape in high velocity back to safer locations far from threats.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing lower approach velocity and higher escape velocity during threat exposure.

claim: No sex differences were found in either behavioral assay.
source: No sex differences were found in either behavioral assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) (male n = 17, female n = 15; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Behavior in the shock grid assay is not affected by prior experience in the rat assay.
source: Nevertheless, to determine whether there could be an effect of order, we exposed two cohorts of mice to the rat and shock grid threats in a counterbalanced manner and showed that behavior in the shock grid assay is not affected by prior experience in the rat assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PMd-cck activity was increased near threats relative to control stimuli.
source: Averaged heat maps show PMd-cck activity was increased near the rat and the shock grid during fear retrieval (Figure 2D). Indeed, activity was increased near threats relative to control stimuli (toy rat and shock grid in pre-shock day).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: PMd-cck cells are more active near threats independently of locomotor changes.
source: These comparisons were done when analyzing data at the same speed range (Figure 2E); thus, PMd-cck cells are more active near threats independently of locomotor changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2E, where activity was compared at matched speed values.

claim: PMd-cck cells showed increased activation during risk-assessment stretch-attend postures and during escape in both rat and shock grid assays.
source: Average data show that in both assays PMd-cck cells showed increased activation during risk-assessment stretch-attend postures and during escape, while a decrease in activity was displayed during freezing (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2G–I.

claim: PMd-cck cells showed a decrease in activity during freezing in both rat and shock grid assays.
source: Average data show that in both assays PMd-cck cells showed increased activation during risk-assessment stretch-attend postures and during escape, while a decrease in activity was displayed during freezing (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2G–I.

claim: The total distance of each escape was correlated with PMd-cck activation during exposure to threats, but not control stimuli.
source: Furthermore, the total distance of each escape was correlated with PMd-cck activation during exposure to threats, but not control stimuli (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2J.

claim: PMd-cck cells are quickly activated by proximity to threat and escape, during exposure to both innate and conditioned threats.
source: These results show that PMd-cck cells are quickly activated by proximity to threat and escape, during exposure to both innate and conditioned threats.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing PMd-cck activation near threats and during escape.

claim: PMd-cck cells displayed relatively high membrane input resistance (484 ± 64 MOhms).
source: In agreement with this view, PMd-cck cells displayed relatively high membrane input resistance (484 ± 64 MOhms) and low rheobase, which is the minimum current required to elicit an action potential (38.3 ± 6.1 pA) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: PMd-cck cells displayed low rheobase (38.3 ± 6.1 pA).
source: In agreement with this view, PMd-cck cells displayed relatively high membrane input resistance (484 ± 64 MOhms) and low rheobase, which is the minimum current required to elicit an action potential (38.3 ± 6.1 pA) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Fairly minor excitatory input is enough to activate PMd-cck cells.
source: These results indicate that fairly minor excitatory input is enough to activate these cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the biophysical properties (high input resistance and low rheobase) of PMd-cck cells.

claim: PMd-cck cells may be rapidly activated in the presence of threats.
source: These biophysical characteristics suggest that these cells may be rapidly activated in the presence of threats.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the biophysical properties of PMd-cck cells.

claim: A large fraction of PMd-cck cells are active during defensive behaviors.
source: Using a generalized linear model (GLM), we identified a large fraction of PMd-cck cells that are active during these behaviors (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: Escape activated the largest number of PMd-cck cells.
source: The behavior that activated the largest and smallest number of PMd-cck cells was, respectively, escape and freezing (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: Freezing activated the smallest number of PMd-cck cells.
source: The behavior that activated the largest and smallest number of PMd-cck cells was, respectively, escape and freezing (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: PMd-cck ensemble activity could be used to decode ongoing escape, but not other behaviors.
source: Further supporting a role for PMd-cck cells in escape, we show that ensemble activity could be used to decode ongoing escape, but not other behaviors (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3G.

claim: PMd-cck activity could predict escape from innate and conditioned threats several seconds prior to escape onset.
source: Indeed, PMd-cck activity could predict escape from innate and conditioned threats several seconds prior to escape onset. However, ensemble activity could not predict movement away from control stimuli (toy rat and shock grid in pre-shock day) (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3H.

claim: PMd-cck ensemble activity could not predict movement away from control stimuli.
source: Indeed, PMd-cck activity could predict escape from innate and conditioned threats several seconds prior to escape onset. However, ensemble activity could not predict movement away from control stimuli (toy rat and shock grid in pre-shock day) (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3H.

claim: PMd-cck activity can specifically predict future escape from threats, but not moving away from objects in general.
source: These data show that PMd-cck activity can specifically predict future escape from threats, but not moving away from objects in general.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing PMd-cck activity predicts escape from threats but not movement away from control stimuli.

claim: A higher fraction of PMd cells showed activity significantly correlated with escape speed for threat than control stimuli.
source: A higher fraction of PMd cells showed activity significantly correlated with escape speed for threat than control stimuli (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3I.

claim: For escape speed-correlated cells, the mutual information between escape speed and calcium signal is significantly greater during threat than control.
source: Additionally, for these escape speed-correlated cells, the mutual information between escape speed and calcium signal is significantly greater during threat than control (Figure 3K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3K.

claim: PMd-cck activity is related to defensive escape and speed in the presence of threat, rather than general locomotion.
source: These data indicate that PMd-cck activity is related to defensive escape and speed in the presence of threat, rather than general locomotion.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing PMd-cck activity correlates with escape speed during threat but not control conditions.

claim: The error of position decoding using PMd-cck ensemble activity was smaller in threat than in control assays.
source: Strikingly, the error of position decoding was both smaller in threat than in control assays and significantly less than chance error (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A–B.

claim: The error of position decoding using PMd-cck ensemble activity was significantly less than chance error.
source: Strikingly, the error of position decoding was both smaller in threat than in control assays and significantly less than chance error (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A–B.

claim: PMd-cck cells represent distance to threat more prominently than distance to control objects.
source: These results show that PMd-cck cells represent distance to threat more prominently than distance to control objects.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing better position decoding accuracy during threat than control conditions.

claim: PMd-cck activity could be used to decode velocity during threat exposure with higher accuracy than during exposure to control stimuli.
source: Indeed, PMd-cck activity could be used to decode velocity during threat exposure with higher accuracy than during exposure to control stimuli (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The error for predicted velocity is lower for decoding velocity away from threat compared to velocity toward threat.
source: Indeed, averaged data across mice show that the error for predicted velocity is lower for decoding velocity away from threat compared to velocity toward threat.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Only velocity away from threat can be predicted with an error significantly less than chance.
source: Moreover, only velocity away from threat can be predicted with an error significantly less than chance (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C,D.

claim: PMd-cck cells represent key kinematic variables related to rapid escape from threats.
source: These data show that PMd-cck cells represent key kinematic variables related to rapid escape from threats.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing PMd-cck cells encode position, escape speed, and velocity away from threats.

claim: CNO produced hyperpolarization in hM4Di-expressing PMd-cck cells.
source: We confirmed that the hM4Di receptor ligand clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) produced hyperpolarization (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Inhibition of PMd-cck cells in CNO-treated mice decreased escape velocity from both threats.
source: Inhibition of PMd-cck cells in CNO-treated mice decreased escape velocity from both threats, in line with our prediction (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Inhibiting PMd-cck cells did not change velocity while mice moved away from control safe stimuli.
source: Importantly, inhibiting these cells did not change velocity, while mice moved away from control safe stimuli (toy rat and shock grid prior to fear conditioning) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibiting PMd-cck cells did not change freezing or stretch-attend postures.
source: This manipulation did not change freezing or stretch-attend postures (Figure 5D), showing PMd-cck activity is selectively required for escape, rather than defensive behaviors in general.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: PMd-cck activity is selectively required for escape, rather than defensive behaviors in general.
source: This manipulation did not change freezing or stretch-attend postures (Figure 5D), showing PMd-cck activity is selectively required for escape, rather than defensive behaviors in general.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing PMd-cck inhibition affects escape but not other defensive behaviors.

claim: Optogenetic activation of ChR2-expressing PMd-cck cells caused an increase in speed.
source: Indeed, optogenetic activation of ChR2-expressing PMd-cck cells caused an increase in speed, but not in the amount of freezing or stretch-attend postures (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Optogenetic activation of ChR2-expressing PMd-cck cells did not increase the amount of freezing or stretch-attend postures.
source: Indeed, optogenetic activation of ChR2-expressing PMd-cck cells caused an increase in speed, but not in the amount of freezing or stretch-attend postures (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Blue light delivery caused increased fos expression in the PMd, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST) and anteromedial ventral thalamus (amv) following optogenetic activation of PMd-cck cells.
source: Representative images show that blue light delivery caused increased fos expression in the PMd, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST) and anteromedial ventral thalamus (amv). Other regions, such as the central amygdala (Cea) and the dentate gyrus (DG) did not show increased fos expression following PMD-cck optogenetic stimulation. (scale bar: 100 µm)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: The central amygdala (Cea) and the dentate gyrus (DG) did not show increased fos expression following PMd-cck optogenetic stimulation.
source: Representative images show that blue light delivery caused increased fos expression in the PMd, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST) and anteromedial ventral thalamus (amv). Other regions, such as the central amygdala (Cea) and the dentate gyrus (DG) did not show increased fos expression following PMD-cck optogenetic stimulation. (scale bar: 100 µm)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: PMd activation increased fos expression in regions that it projects to, such as the amv and the dlPAG.
source: PMd activation increased fos expression in regions that it projects to, such as the amv and the dlPAG.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Other nuclei critical for defensive behaviors, such as the basolateral amygdala, lateral septum, and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, were activated following PMd-cck optogenetic stimulation.
source: Interestingly, other nuclei critical for defensive behaviors, such as the basolateral amygdala, lateral septum, and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, were also activated (Figure 6C), even though they are not innervated by the PMd (Canteras and Swanson, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C and citation to prior work by Canteras and Swanson, 1992.

claim: The basolateral amygdala, lateral septum, and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis are not innervated by the PMd.
source: Interestingly, other nuclei critical for defensive behaviors, such as the basolateral amygdala, lateral septum, and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, were also activated (Figure 6C), even though they are not innervated by the PMd (Canteras and Swanson, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Canteras and Swanson, 1992.

claim: Striatal regions such as the caudate nucleus were activated following PMd-cck optogenetic stimulation, possibly due to the hyperlocomotion and escape-related actions observed during optogenetic stimulation.
source: Striatal regions were also activated, such as the caudate nucleus, possibly due to the hyperlocomotion and escape-related actions observed during optogenetic stimulation.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the experimental data showing caudate nucleus activation and observed hyperlocomotion.

claim: The dentate gyrus and the PMd-adjacent ventral PMd did not show increases in fos expression following PMd stimulation.
source: Importantly, not all regions were engaged, showing functional specificity. For example, the dentate gyrus and the PMd-adjacent ventral PMd did not show increases in fos expression following PMd stimulation (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: PMd-cck cells can recruit a broad network of threat-activated regions, which may contribute to a transition to a defensive state.
source: These data show that PMd-cck cells can recruit a broad network of threat-activated regions, which may contribute to a transition to a defensive state.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the experimental data showing activation of multiple threat-related regions following PMd-cck stimulation.

claim: The amv has head direction cells.
source: The amv has head direction cells (Bassett et al., 2007) and is a region critical for threat-conditioned contextual memory (Carvalho-Netto et al., 2010) and spatial navigation (Jankowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Bassett et al., 2007.

claim: The amv is a region critical for threat-conditioned contextual memory.
source: The amv has head direction cells (Bassett et al., 2007) and is a region critical for threat-conditioned contextual memory (Carvalho-Netto et al., 2010) and spatial navigation (Jankowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Carvalho-Netto et al., 2010.

claim: The amv is a region critical for spatial navigation.
source: The amv has head direction cells (Bassett et al., 2007) and is a region critical for threat-conditioned contextual memory (Carvalho-Netto et al., 2010) and spatial navigation (Jankowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Jankowski et al., 2013.

claim: The amv is necessary for the acquisition of contextual fear elicited by predators.
source: The amv is also necessary for the acquisition of contextual fear elicited by predators (Carvalho-Netto et al., 2010), demonstrating this region has a role in defensive behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Carvalho-Netto et al., 2010.

claim: The dlPAG is a critical node in the escape network.
source: In contrast, the dlPAG is a critical node in the escape network (Del-Ben and Graeff, 2009; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Del-Ben and Graeff, 2009 and Tovote et al., 2016.

claim: DLPAG activity increased during escape from the rat.
source: DLPAG activity increased during escape from the rat (Figure 7C), in agreement with prior work showing this region is active during escape from innate threats (Deng et al., 2016; Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7C and citations to prior work by Deng et al., 2016 and Evans et al., 2018.

claim: The dlPAG showed increased activity during exposure to the fear conditioned shock grid during fear retrieval.
source: However, the dlPAG also showed increased activity during exposure to the fear conditioned shock grid during fear retrieval (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7D,E.

claim: The amv was active during escape from both threat modalities.
source: Surprisingly, like the dlPAG, the amv was also active during escape from both threat modalities (Figure 7G–I), even though there are no prior reports implicating the amv in escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7G–I.

claim: Inhibition of the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG with green light decreased escape velocity in both assays.
source: Inhibition of the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG with green light decreased escape velocity in both assays (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8D.

claim: Inhibition of the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG did not alter other defensive behaviors such as freezing or stretch-attend postures.
source: This manipulation did not alter other defensive behaviors such as freezing or stretch-attend postures (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8D.

claim: Inhibition of the PMd-cck projection to the amv did not change any defensive behavioral measure in either assay.
source: In contrast, inhibition of the PMd-cck projection to the amv did not change any defensive behavioral measure in either assay (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8E.

claim: The activity in the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG, but not to the amv, is necessary for normal escape vigor during exposure to both innate and conditioned threats.
source: These data show that the activity in the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG, but not to the amv, is necessary for normal escape vigor during exposure to both innate and conditioned threats.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing PMd-dlPAG inhibition affects escape speed while PMd-amv inhibition does not.

claim: The mutual information between the PMd and dlPAG is higher during exposure to threat than control assays.
source: Using the mutual information metric – an information-theoretic quantity that reflects the amount of information obtained for one variable by observing another variable – we found that the mutual information between the PMd and dlPAG is higher during exposure to threat than control assays (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 9D.

claim: The mutual information between the PMd and dlPAG is higher during exposure to threat than control assays even when escapes were removed.
source: This was also true when escapes were removed, indicating that the mutual information change seen is related to threat exposure, rather than specific defensive behaviors (Figure 9D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 9D.

claim: The PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG is unilateral.
source: As the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG is unilateral (Figure 9—figure supplement 1; Canteras and Swanson, 1992), performing contralateral recordings ensures that dlPAG-syn cell body signals are not contaminated by signals from GCaMP-expressing PMd-cck axons terminating in the dlPAG.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior work by Canteras and Swanson, 1992.

claim: The dlPAG does not project to the PMd.
source: The dlPAG does not project to the PMd (Comoli et al., 2000); thus, there is no risk of recording signals from GCaMP-expressing dlPAG axons in the PMd.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Comoli et al., 2000.

claim: The HTH–PAG pathway responded more strongly to aversive images than non-aversive images.
source: This HTH–PAG pathway responded more strongly to aversive images than non-aversive images and its activation also scaled monotonically with aversiveness (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human fMRI studies presented in Figure 10C.

claim: Activation of the HTH–PAG pathway scaled monotonically with aversiveness.
source: This HTH–PAG pathway responded more strongly to aversive images than non-aversive images and its activation also scaled monotonically with aversiveness (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human fMRI studies presented in Figure 10C.

claim: Portions of medial posterior hypothalamus (neighboring the mammillary bodies) were most consistently associated with PAG activation.
source: Examination of the multi-voxel patterns contributing to the HTH–PAG pathway revealed that portions of medial posterior hypothalamus (neighboring the mammillary bodies) were most consistently associated with PAG activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human fMRI studies presented in Figure 10A.

claim: Activation of the HTH–PAG pathway is selective and does not correlate with activation of the amygdala–PAG pathway.
source: We also show that activation of the HTH–PAG pathway is selective and does not correlate with activation of a different major subcortical input pathway to the PAG, such as the amygdala–PAG pathway (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human fMRI studies presented in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Functional connectivity in a hypothalamic-PAG pathway is increased in humans during aversive situations.
source: Thus, these data show that functional connectivity in a hypothalamic-PAG pathway is increased in humans during aversive situations, in agreement with our results in mice showing that the hypothalamic to brainstem PMd–dlPAG pathway is engaged during exposure to aversive threats (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from human fMRI studies and mouse experiments.

claim: The PMd is anatomically the source of the most prominent input to the dlPAG.
source: The PMd is anatomically the source of the most prominent input to the dlPAG (Del-Ben and Graeff, 2009; Lovick, 2000; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Del-Ben and Graeff, 2009, Lovick, 2000, and Tovote et al., 2016.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PMd-cck cells activates a broad network of regions involved in defensive behaviors.
source: Furthermore, optogenetic activation of PMd-cck cells activates a broad network of regions involved in defensive behaviors (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: PMd-cck cells play a key role in controlling escape vigor, during exposure to both innate and conditioned threats.
source: We now show PMd-cck cells play a key role in controlling escape vigor, during exposure to both innate and conditioned threats.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined experimental data showing PMd-cck cells are activated during escape, predict escape, and their inhibition decreases escape speed.

claim: PMd-cck cells represented distance to threat, but not distance to control stimuli.
source: Interestingly, PMd-cck cells also represented distance to threat, but not distance to control stimuli (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: PMd input to the dlPAG may contribute to the encoding of distance to threat and related kinematic variables in dlPAG cells.
source: PMd input to the dlPAG may thus contribute to the encoding of distance to threat and related kinematic variables in dlPAG cells as we recently reported (Reis et al., 2021; Reis et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the experimental data and citations to prior work by Reis et al., 2021.

claim: Prior work using excitotoxic PMd lesions and local infusions of muscimol in rats reported large decreases in freezing.
source: Prior work using excitotoxic PMd lesions and local infusions of muscimol in rats reported large decreases in freezing (Cezario et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Cezario et al., 2008.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of PMd-cck cells in mice revealed only deficits in escape.
source: In contrast, our chemogenetic inhibition of PMd-cck cells in mice revealed only deficits in escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The PMd, as well as the dlPAG, participate in defensive responses elicited by both innate and shock-based conditioned threats.
source: Interestingly, our data show that the PMd, as well as the dlPAG, participate in defensive responses elicited by both innate and shock-based conditioned threats.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing PMd and dlPAG activity during exposure to both innate and conditioned threats.

claim: The dlPAG is activated during exposure to shock-conditioned auditory tones and contexts.
source: For example, the dlPAG is activated during exposure to shock-conditioned auditory tones and contexts (Carrive et al., 1997; Watson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Carrive et al., 1997 and Watson et al., 2016.

claim: Neurotransmission of cannabinoids, CRF, glutamate, and nitric oxide in the dlPAG have been shown to be necessary for contextual freezing.
source: Furthermore, neurotransmission of cannabinoids (Resstel et al., 2008), CRF (Borelli et al., 2013), glutamate, and nitric oxide (Aguiar et al., 2014) have been shown to be necessary for contextual freezing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Resstel et al., 2008, Borelli et al., 2013, and Aguiar et al., 2014.

claim: The PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG modulates escape velocity from conditioned threats.
source: We now show that the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG modulates escape velocity from conditioned threats, broadening the role of this circuit to include escape from learned threats.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8.

claim: dlPAG cells represent distance from a learned conditioned threatening shock grid during fear retrieval.
source: More recently, we showed that dlPAG cells represent distance from a learned conditioned threatening shock grid during fear retrieval, further supporting a role for this region in mediating defense induced by conditioned threats (Reis et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Reis et al., 2021.

claim: The dlPAG is bidirectionally connected with diverse forebrain regions.
source: The dlPAG is bidirectionally connected with diverse forebrain regions (Motta et al., 2017), while the PMd receives strong input from the medial prefrontal cortex (Comoli et al., 2000), which may explain how these regions respond to conditioned threats.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Motta et al., 2017 and Comoli et al., 2000.

claim: The PMd receives strong input from the medial prefrontal cortex.
source: The dlPAG is bidirectionally connected with diverse forebrain regions (Motta et al., 2017), while the PMd receives strong input from the medial prefrontal cortex (Comoli et al., 2000), which may explain how these regions respond to conditioned threats.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Comoli et al., 2000.

claim: During contextual fear retrieval tests, rats showed increased PMd fos expression if they had free access to the conditioning chamber, but not if they were confined to this chamber.
source: Intriguingly, during contextual fear retrieval tests, rats showed increased PMd fos expression if they had free access to the conditioning chamber, but not if they were confined to this chamber (Viellard et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Viellard et al., 2016.

claim: Information about innate predatory threats are likely conveyed to the PMd by other members of the hypothalamic predatory defense circuit, such as the VMHdm and the anterior hypothalamus.
source: Information about innate predatory threats are likely conveyed to the PMd by other members of the hypothalamic predatory defense circuit, such as the VMHdm and the anterior hypothalamus (Cezario et al., 2008; Comoli et al., 2000; Silva et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is speculation based on citations to prior work by Cezario et al., 2008, Comoli et al., 2000, and Silva et al., 2013.

claim: The PMd–dlPAG circuit is not merely responding to external threatening sensory cues.
source: Nevertheless, our data show that the PMd–dlPAG circuit is not merely responding to external threatening sensory cues.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing the circuit is involved in escape from conditioned stimuli during fear retrieval.

claim: The involvement of the PMd–dlPAG circuit in escape from conditioned stimuli during fear retrieval shows that these structures can be affected by long-term fear memories.
source: Rather, the involvement of this circuit in escape from conditioned stimuli during fear retrieval shows that these structures can be affected by long-term fear memories, illustrating that evolutionarily ancient structures can also display experience-dependent roles in behavior.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing the circuit is involved in escape from conditioned stimuli during fear retrieval.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of the PMd–amv projection decreased the number of escapes elicited by a predator rat in environments requiring sophisticated three-dimensional spatial navigation to escape.
source: Intriguingly, our prior data showed that optogenetic inhibition of the PMd–amv projection decreased the number of escapes elicited by a predator rat in environments requiring sophisticated three-dimensional spatial navigation to escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Wang et al., 2021 (implied by context).

claim: PMd–amv activity was not necessary for stereotyped jumps in the presence of the panicogenic agent CO2.
source: However, PMd–amv activity was not necessary for stereotyped jumps in the presence of the panicogenic agent CO2 (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Inhibition of the PMd-cck projection to the amv did not alter any defensive behavioral metrics induced by a rat in a simple environment.
source: We now show inhibition of the PMd-cck projection to the amv did not alter any defensive behavioral metrics induced by a rat in a simple environment (Figure 1), where the animal does not need a complex three-dimensional understanding of the environmental layout to escape (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 8D.

claim: The role of the PMd–amv circuit is related to complex navigation during threat exposure.
source: As inhibition of the PMd–amv projection impaired escape from a predatory rat only when flight required complex navigation, we argue that the role of this circuit is related to complex navigation during threat exposure, supporting our second interpretation above.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing PMd–amv inhibition affects escape only in complex environments.

claim: The amv's role in defensive behavior is related to contextual memory-associated behaviors rather than the execution of escape or freezing.
source: These data agree with prior work that indicate the amv's role in defensive behavior is related to contextual memory-associated behaviors rather than the execution of escape or freezing (Carvalho-Netto et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Carvalho-Netto et al., 2010.

claim: A homologous functional pathway to the rodent PMd-dlPAG may exist in humans that is at least partially identifiable from fMRI data.
source: Intriguingly, our fMRI data indicate that a hypothalamic-PAG pathway has increased activity in humans viewing aversive images (Figure 10). A homologous functional pathway to the rodent PMd-dlPAG may exist in humans that is at least partially identifiable from fMRI data.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the experimental data from human fMRI studies.

claim: HTH and dlPAG were positively correlated in every participant in out-of-sample tests.
source: In out-of-sample tests in new participants, HTH and dlPAG were positively correlated in every participant and tracked the reported intensity of negative emotion elicited by images.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human fMRI studies.

claim: HTH and dlPAG activity tracked the reported intensity of negative emotion elicited by images.
source: In out-of-sample tests in new participants, HTH and dlPAG were positively correlated in every participant and tracked the reported intensity of negative emotion elicited by images.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human fMRI studies.

claim: The location of the hypothalamic nucleus involved in the HTH-PAG pathway is in the posterior medial hypothalamus, similar to the rodent PMd.
source: However, the location of the nucleus is in the posterior medial hypothalamus, similar to the rodent PMd, suggesting the possibility that a circuit analogous to the PMd–dlPAG projection may exist in humans.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the experimental data from human fMRI studies showing the location of the hypothalamic activation.

claim: The PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG modulates escape velocity during exposure to both innate and conditioned threats.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG modulates escape velocity during exposure to both innate and conditioned threats, and the results suggest a similar pathway may be active during exposure to aversive situations in humans.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined experimental data from mouse and human studies.

claim: A similar pathway to the PMd-dlPAG may be active during exposure to aversive situations in humans.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that the PMd-cck projection to the dlPAG modulates escape velocity during exposure to both innate and conditioned threats, and the results suggest a similar pathway may be active during exposure to aversive situations in humans.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the combined experimental data from mouse and human studies.
